description:
Can You See Jupiter's Moons Tonight?

Episode 91 of a daily journey through the universe. 🪐
Season 6 begins with Jupiter at opposition on February 10 to 11, 2027: the king of planets shines at magnitude −2.6 in the constellation Leo, rises at sunset and stays up all night. How to find it, and how to see four of its moons with simple binoculars.

➡️ Tomorrow, Episode 92: Next stop, the Great Red Spot. A storm bigger than our whole planet.
Start from Episode 1 "Leaving Earth" on the channel.
Follow so you don't miss a stop. A new episode every day.

segments.text: Tonight, you can see Jupiter's moons with just binoculars. Here's how.
On February tenth and eleventh, Jupiter reaches opposition. Earth passes right between Jupiter and the Sun.
segments.headline: Earth in the middle

segments.text: That means Jupiter rises as the Sun sets, and shines all night long.

visual.query: Jupiter bright planet night sky photograph
visual.commons: Jupiter bright planet night sky photograph

segments.headline: Up all night

segments.text: It will be brighter than any star in the sky, at magnitude minus two point six.
Look east after sunset, in the constellation Leo. That bright, steady light that doesn't twinkle? That's Jupiter. And just a week later, Mars joins it in Leo.
segments.headline: Look east, in Leo

segments.text: Even at its closest, Jupiter is about six hundred and fifty million kilometers away. Its light takes thirty-six minutes to reach your eyes.
Now grab binoculars and hold them steady. You'll see up to four tiny dots lined up beside it.
segments.headline: Grab binoculars

segments.text: Those are Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. The same moons Galileo saw in sixteen ten, the discovery that proved not everything circles the Earth.
segments.headline: Galileo's moons

segments.text: Watch over a few nights, and they change places as they orbit.
segments.headline: They move every night

segments.text: But with a small telescope, you might spot something else. A dark red eye on Jupiter's face. A storm bigger than Earth. Which part surprised you most? Tell me in the comments, and follow for tomorrow's stop.
